title: Yes means yes
hookLine: don't laugh much or loudly, and avoid swearing oaths when you can (Enchiridion 33)
carry: a word that doesn't need help

lines: I SWEAR. I SWEAR ON MY MOTHER.
THE MORE YOU PILE ON, THE LESS SURE.
cards: I swear I'll be there. I swear on my mother. Hand on heart, I promise.
You stack these up when you want to be believed, and the funny thing is, the more you pile on, the less sure everyone gets.
Someone who says I swear three times in one sentence can end up being the one people double-check.
Section thirty-three keeps sketching a person of character, and today it gets to two small habits: how you laugh, and how you promise.

teach.h: DON'T LAUGH MUCH, OR WITHOUT RESTRAINT.
teach.b: First, laughter. Don't laugh much, Epictetus says, or at many things, or without restraint. That can sound grim, so look closely.

He isn't banning joy. The worry seems to be laughing that runs away with a person: laughing to fit in, laughing at someone, laughing so loudly you're no longer really there. A smile you mean is still in your power.
A roar to impress the room may not be.

teach.h: REFUSE OATHS, AS FAR AS YOU CAN.
teach.b: Then oaths. Refuse to swear an oath, he says, altogether if you can, and if you can't, as far as you can. He doesn't stop to explain.

teach.h: A GOOD WORD NEEDS NO OATH.
teach.b: One way to read it: if your plain word is good, an oath adds nothing. If it isn't, an oath won't fix it. Piling on swears is a quiet admission that a simple yes isn't enough.

So the Stoic aims to be someone whose yes is the whole promise. A neighbor said something close. In the Sermon on the Mount, in the King James Bible, Jesus says: "But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay."
Christians have taken that in different ways.
Quakers, and some Mennonite and Amish communities, decline to swear oaths and affirm instead. Other Christians take oaths in court and office and read the verse as being about honesty.
The United States Constitution makes room for both: a president may swear, or affirm. Two traditions, each in its own house, arriving at the same plain picture: a word that doesn't need help.

how: Some people on a Stoic path avoid oaths and emphatic promises and try to keep their plain word instead; Quakers and some other Christian communities affirm rather than swear.

o: a lucky charm worn to keep a promise safe
a sworn promise, best refused when you can
a curse word blurted out in a moment of anger

games.q: yes means yes — tap the pairs.
p: refuse them as far as you can

s: he says not much, not at many things, not without restraint.
the U.S. Constitution lets a president affirm instead of swear
the oath of office reads swear, or affirm.
Epictetus gives a long argument against oaths
he simply says refuse them, altogether if you can; the reasons are one way to read him.

games.q: a friend doubts you'll show up tomorrow. what would Epictetus have you do?
o: swear by everything you hold dear.
say yes plainly, and then show up.
games.why: he says refuse oaths as far as you can. a good word needs no oath, and a bad one isn't fixed by it.

practice: Think of one recent promise, I'll call you back, I'll finish it by Friday, I'll be there, and picture the person you made it to.
Without adding a single I swear, just decide to keep it: no drama, no extra words, just a yes that holds. If there's a promise you can't keep, picture yourself telling them so, simply.

wordCard.voice: Oath. What Epictetus says to refuse as far as you can, letting your plain word carry the promise instead. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: an oath, which Enchiridion 33 says to refuse, altogether if possible.

carryVoice: Your line: a word that doesn't need help. A plain yes can carry the whole promise. Day three hundred sixty-six.
